title: Kubja Carves a Poem in Stone

title_i18n.en: Kubja Carves a Poem in Stone

subtitle: A Poet, a Pillar, and the Birth of a Written Lineage
moral: History lasts longer when memory learns an artful form.

sources.citation: B.L. Rice, Epigraphia Carnatica vol. 7, inscription 176 (1902); F. Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica 8 (1906): 24-36
sources.note: Editions and translations of the Talagunda pillar inscription.

sources.citation: D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilisation, vol. 1, 2nd ed. (1965)
sources.note: Standard epigraphic selection including the inscription.

sources.citation: G.S. Gai, Inscriptions of the Early Kadambas (1996)
sources.note: Modern critical corpus for Kadamba inscriptions and script forms.

panels.shot: low-angle medium shot of Kubja beside a towering stone pillar in a temple courtyard at dusk

dialogue.text: In Talagunda, a court poet named Kubja was ordered to do the unthinkable — turn royal memory into Sanskrit poetry and carve it forever into stone.

panels.shot: wide establishing shot of Talagunda village and Praneshvara temple complex nestled by fields and trees

dialogue.text: Around the mid-5th century, in the quiet settlement of Talagunda, a temple to Praneshvara watched over fields, scholars and scribes as kings rose and fell beyond its trees.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot inside a simple hall, scrolls and palm-leaves laid out, Kubja seated cross-legged

dialogue.text: Among them lived Kubja, a Sanskrit poet and court scholar, trained to weigh each syllable, each image, until language itself felt like finely hammered metal.

panels.shot: medium shot of Kubja in a royal audience hall before an unseen seated king, focus on Kubja’s attentive face

dialogue.text: His patron was Santivarma of the Kadamba line, a king who ruled from Banavasi yet looked to Talagunda’s shrine and scholars as anchors of his family’s story.

panels.shot: close-up on Kubja’s face as he listens, with a faint mix of pride and anxiety

dialogue.speaker: kubja
dialogue.text: You wish your lineage sung in stone, Maharaja? As polished kavya?

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot from behind Kubja, showing courtiers gesturing to a rough granite pillar outside

dialogue.text: Santivarma wanted more than a record of grants and borders. He wanted a crafted poem, thirty and more verses, to bind his house to gods, battles and teachers.

panels.shot: low-angle close-up of Kubja’s hand holding a stylus, hovering over a palm-leaf

dialogue.text: In the Deccan, inscriptions had long marked gifts and victories. But Kubja was asked for something rarer: an inscription shaped like court poetry, in careful Sanskrit meters.

panels.shot: montage-like medium shot showing Kubja reciting to himself, gesturing with fingers as he counts meter

dialogue.text: He chose meters that scholars like Kielhorn would one day list: the tight discipline of anuṣṭubh, the sweep of vasanta-tilaka and others, fitting deity, genealogy and war into rhythm.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Kubja’s face as he imagines the lineage, faint ghostly silhouettes of ancestors implied behind him

dialogue.text: The inscription would tell of Brahmana origins, of a Kadamba ancestor’s insult at Kanchi, of Mayurasharma taking up arms, of kings who followed, of Santivarma himself at the end.

panels.shot: medium shot of Kubja presenting a palm-leaf manuscript to a temple priest or court official in the temple courtyard

dialogue.text: The poet’s task was only half the work. His verses had to move from leaf and tongue to the stubborn grain of granite, letter by letter, without losing their form.

panels.shot: high-angle shot over the shoulder of a stonecutter as he incises the first letters, Kubja supervising

dialogue.text: The script followed the Kadamba stream: rounded, early forms that would one day give rise to later Kannada and related southern scripts, yet here they carried Sanskrit sounds.

panels.shot: extreme close-up of a line of freshly cut Kadamba letters on the pillar, stone dust still clinging

dialogue.text: Each carved syllable bore two memories at once: the polished sound of court Sanskrit, and the visual discipline of a regional script line still finding its own shapes.

panels.shot: medium shot of Kubja and craftsmen working together, pillar partially covered in inscription

dialogue.speaker: kubja
dialogue.text: Do not crowd the meter. The verse must still breathe on stone.

panels.shot: wide shot of the nearly finished pillar standing tall near the Praneshvara temple, villagers watching

dialogue.text: By the time Kubja’s poem reached its final verses, the pillar had become more than stone. It was now a vertical manuscript, raised under open sky, addressed to gods, men and time.

panels.shot: close-up on Kubja’s face as he reads aloud from the stone, eyes tracing the letters

dialogue.text: The inscription itself would one day state that Kubja composed this kavya and had it placed on stone by Santivarma’s order, tying author, patron and object in a single claim.

panels.shot: medium shot of Santivarma and Kubja before the pillar, king’s hand resting on the stone

dialogue.text: For Santivarma, the pillar was a public answer to doubt: here was a clear genealogy, a shaped past, a declaration that the Kadambas stood not by accident but by cosmic and learned design.

panels.shot: soft-focus shot of the pillar weathering over time, subtle changes in surroundings suggesting centuries passing

dialogue.text: Centuries would pass. Dynasties around Banavasi would rise, fracture and vanish, but Kubja’s verses, now mute lines of stone, stayed in the village wind.

panels.shot: modern-era scholar in the foreground copying the inscription, pillar behind; Kubja’s faint spectral figure suggested beside the pillar

dialogue.text: In the 19th and 20th centuries, editors like Rice, Kielhorn and Sircar would lean close to these letters, teasing out meters, names and dates, hearing Kubja’s craft through their own training.

panels.shot: interior shot of a modern archaeologist documenting the 2013 Talagunda balustrade find, pillar visible outside through a doorway

dialogue.text: New finds at Talagunda, like the 2013 balustrade, would add further layers to the site’s language history, but Kubja’s pillar remained the clearest, self-conscious poem of power there.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of the pillar today, tourists and students looking up, sky bright above

dialogue.text: Today we read it as history: a source for Mayurasharma and the Kadambas. Yet it is also an early Deccan example of something quieter — history cast deliberately as artful kavya.

panels.shot: final contemplative medium shot of Kubja’s imagined figure seated beneath the pillar, stylus resting on his knee, looking outward

dialogue.text: Kubja’s work reminds us that power lasts longer when it learns a form, and that in the meeting of meter, script and stone, memory gains a body that can outlive its makers.
